specAnchors.text: describe the evolution of stars with a mass larger than the Sun

primer.text: High-mass stars live fast and die loud: a shorter main sequence, then a red supergiant, then a supernova — the gigantic explosion that forges the heaviest elements — leaving behind a neutron star, or a black hole for the most massive of all.

modules.title: Red supergiants
sourceHeadings: The life cycle of larger stars
modules.opening: Past the main sequence, a high-mass star swells into a red supergiant. Compared with a Sun-like star it burns through its hydrogen in a shorter time, and where the solar-mass star fuses helium into carbon, the bigger star carries the build-up on to iron.
keyPoints: A high-mass star becomes a red supergiant after the main sequence.
Higher-mass stars leave the main sequence sooner — a shorter stay before the supergiant turn.
Helium fusion yields carbon in lower-mass stars; higher-mass cores carry the build-up on to iron.
As the supergiant expands, its surface cools and reddens.

low.restatement: Big star, brief youth: shorter main sequence, then the red supergiant swelling.
low.analogy: A fireworks rocket versus a candle: the bigger the charge, the brighter and the shorter the show.
low.examPointer: Contrast pairs score: solar-mass/carbon versus high-mass/iron.

medium.restatement: Mass drives both the clock and the chemistry: shorter main sequence, helium fused beyond carbon up to iron.
medium.analogy: A bigger bonfire: hotter core, faster consumption, larger glow.
medium.examPointer: 'Red supergiant' is one hyphenated concept — write it exactly.

modules.title: Supernovae
modules.opening: When fusion inside the red supergiant can no longer continue, the core collapses suddenly and a gigantic explosion — a supernova — blasts the star apart. At the centre a dense neutron star forms, while the outer remnants are ejected into space as new clouds of dust and gas; the heaviest elements are forged here and scattered.
keyPoints: When fusion cannot continue, the core collapses suddenly and a gigantic explosion — a supernova — occurs.
The explosion's centre condenses into a dense body: the neutron star.
Outer remnants blast into space as fresh clouds of dust and gas — nebulae.
Supernovae forge the heaviest elements and scatter them into space.

low.restatement: Fusion fails → sudden core collapse → gigantic explosion → neutron star centre, nebula outskirts.
low.analogy: A walnut crushed in a press: the hard core stays as a dense lump while the shell splinters across the room.
low.examPointer: Carry the element story: heaviest elements formed in the supernova and ejected.

medium.restatement: The supernova is a forge and a delivery service at once: heavy elements made, then scattered into future nebulae.
medium.analogy: A bakery explosion that showers the street with fresh bread — destructive and generative in one blast.
medium.examPointer: 'Neutron star' at the centre and 'nebulae' from the remnants — two distinct products, two marks.

modules.title: Neutron stars and black holes
modules.opening: The supernova leaves a neutron star at its centre — but for the most massive stars the story continues: the neutron core keeps collapsing under gravity until it forms a black hole — an object of such extreme density that its gravity traps even light.
keyPoints: A neutron star forms at the centre of a supernova.
In the most massive stars the neutron star continues collapsing under gravity.
The continued collapse forms a black hole.
A black hole is extremely dense — its gravity traps everything, light included.

low.restatement: Supernova leaves a neutron star; extra mass crushes it into a black hole.
low.analogy: A fist closing: the bigger the hand (mass), the tighter the squeeze until even light cannot slip between the fingers.
low.examPointer: 'Not even light can escape' is the required black hole phrase.

medium.restatement: Gravity's final word: beyond the neutron star stage, collapse continues until light itself is trapped.
medium.analogy: A whirlpool: the heaviest drain pulls everything under, even the spray.
medium.examPointer: Name gravity as the driver of the continued collapse.

glossary.definition: The swollen, cooled stage of a high-mass star after its main sequence.
The gigantic explosion following sudden core collapse, forging the heaviest elements.
The dense body formed at the centre of a supernova.
An extremely dense object with gravity so strong not even light escapes.

figures.alt: Lifecycle of a high-mass star: cloud of gas, protostar, massive main sequence star, red supergiant, supernova, then neutron star or black hole.
figures.sourceHeading: The life cycle of larger stars
figures.caption: The high-mass path runs through a supergiant and a supernova
